You revise one blog article for an online shop. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, the current draft, and the problems found in it. Return the whole article again with every problem fixed. Where a sentence cannot be backed by a fact, remove it or say less; never add a citation the fact does not support. Keep what was good.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: How to Use a French Press: A Step-by-Step Guide to a Clean, Full-Bodied Cup
Meta description: Learn how to use a French press: ratio, coarse grind, water temperature, steep time and plunging technique for a clean, full-bodied cup at home.
Slug: how-to-use-a-french-press

To use a French press, combine coarsely ground coffee with water just off the boil at a ratio of roughly 1:15 to 1:16, steep for about 4 minutes, skim the crust, press slowly and pour all of the coffee out straight away [G]. Each of those steps controls either extraction or clarity. Get them right and you keep the heavy, rounded body the press is known for without the muddy, bitter finish that gives it a bad name. The method in full, and the reasons behind each step, follow below.

## Why the French Press Makes Such a Full-Bodied Cup

The French press is an immersion brewer. Instead of water flowing through a bed of coffee, as in pour-over, all of the grounds sit in all of the water for the whole brew. Extraction happens evenly and fairly forgivingly, because every particle has the same contact time.

When the steep is done, a metal mesh pushes the grounds to the bottom and holds them there. Unlike a paper filter, a metal mesh lets coffee oils and some very fine particles pass into the cup. Those oils and fines are what give press coffee its weight and texture. They are also why technique matters: too many fines and the cup turns gritty and over-extracted.

Our [French Press](P1) is an immersion brewer built around a borosilicate glass beaker held in a stainless steel frame [F2, F4, F5]. It uses a four-layer mesh filter to separate the grounds from the brewed coffee [F7].

{{P1}}

## What You Need: Ratio, Water and Batch Size

A French press rewards measuring. Brewing by weight rather than by scoops removes the biggest source of inconsistency, because scoops vary with grind size and bean density.

- **Ratio:** start at about 1 g of coffee to 15–16 g of water, which works out to roughly 60–65 g of coffee per litre of water [G].
- **Water temperature:** aim for about 93–96 °C, which is water left to rest for around 30 seconds after boiling [G].
- **Scale and timer:** weigh the coffee and the water, and time the steep, so you can repeat a cup you like.

Water weighs about 1 g per millilitre, so you can pour straight onto a scale and read the volume in grams [G].

Our French Press has a capacity of 1 litre and makes about 4 mugs [F1, F6]. You do not have to fill it every time; the ratio simply scales with the amount you brew:

- One mug: about 16 g of coffee to 250 g of water [G].
- Half a press: about 32 g of coffee to 500 g of water [G].
- A full batch: about 60–65 g of coffee to 1,000 g of water [G].

Remember that the grounds take up space, so a full batch will sit a little below the rim once everything is in the beaker. If the result tastes too strong or too weak, change the ratio before you change anything else.

## Get the Grind Right: Coarse and Even

Grind size is the single biggest lever in French press brewing. Because the coffee sits in water for minutes rather than seconds, it needs a coarse grind, roughly the texture of coarse sea salt or breadcrumbs.

Uniformity matters as much as size. A grind that is too fine, or full of dust, over-extracts and pushes sludge through the mesh, giving a bitter, silty cup. A grind that is too coarse under-extracts and tastes thin and sour. A burr grinder produces far more consistent particles than a blade grinder, which chops unevenly and creates both boulders and powder in the same dose.

Grind just before you brew. Ground coffee loses aroma quickly, and the press, with its long contact time and full-bodied style, shows off fresh aromatics well.

Our [Hand Grinder](P2) is a manual grinder with 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F11, F12]. It has external click adjustment with 30 settings, ranging from espresso at the fine end to French press at the coarse end [F13, F14]. That dedicated coarse range makes it easy to return to the same press setting every morning [F14].

The Hand Grinder holds 25 g of beans, so for a full press you will need to grind in batches [F15]. Simply weigh out the total dose, grind it in portions and tip each one into the beaker. For larger daily batches, browse our [grinders](L1) for electric options.

{{P2}}

## Step by Step: Bloom, Steep, Break the Crust, Plunge

With your coffee weighed and ground, the brew itself is simple:

1. **Preheat.** Rinse the beaker with hot water and discard it, so the glass does not pull heat from the brew.
2. **Add the grounds.** Tip the ground coffee into the empty beaker and set it on your scale.
3. **Pour all the water.** Pour steadily so all the grounds are saturated, adding the full weight of water within about 30 seconds [G].
4. **Stir gently.** Give the slurry a light stir so no dry clumps float on top. Fresh coffee will bloom and rise as it releases gas.
5. **Steep.** Rest the lid on top without pressing and let it steep for 4 minutes [G].
6. **Break the crust.** Stir the floating layer of grounds gently so most of it sinks, then use two spoons to skim off the foam and any remaining floaters.
7. **Let it settle (optional).** Waiting a further 3–5 minutes lets more fines sink to the bottom, giving a noticeably cleaner cup with little loss of heat [G].
8. **Press slowly.** Lower the plunger gently and stop just above the bed of grounds.

The final step deserves care. Pressing hard or fast forces fines through the mesh and churns up the bed, which adds grit and bitterness. On our French Press, a slow, steady press lets the four-layer mesh filter do its job without being overwhelmed [F7]. Stopping above the grounds rather than crushing them keeps the sediment where it belongs.

## Pour Immediately for a Cleaner Cup

Pressing does not stop extraction. The grounds at the bottom are still in contact with coffee, and the longer it sits, the more bitter and astringent it becomes. Decant everything as soon as you have pressed, either into cups or into a carafe or thermal jug.

Leave the last bit behind. The final portion in the beaker holds the highest concentration of fines and sludge, so stop pouring when you reach it rather than tipping the press upside down.

Once you have a baseline, adjust one variable at a time:

- **Bitter, harsh or drying:** grind coarser or shorten the steep.
- **Sour, thin or hollow:** grind finer or lengthen the steep.
- **Too strong or too weak, but balanced:** change the ratio of coffee to water.
- **Gritty or muddy:** use a more even grind, skim the crust thoroughly, let it settle longer and press more slowly.

## Choosing Beans for French Press

The press emphasises body, sweetness and texture, so coffees with chocolate, caramel and nutty notes tend to taste rich and rounded. Brighter, fruitier coffees also work well and gain a heavier mouthfeel than they would through a paper filter.

For a classic, comforting press cup, our [Colombia Huila](P3) is a washed, medium-roast coffee with tasting notes of red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F19, F28, F30]. It comes in 250 g and 1 kg sizes [F22].

{{P3}}

If you want a more vivid cup, our [Ethiopia Guji](P4) is a natural-process, light-roast coffee with tasting notes of blueberry, dark chocolate and jasmine [F39, F40, F41]. It is available as whole bean, which is the best choice if you grind fresh for each brew [F34].

{{P4}}

Whatever you choose, buying whole bean and grinding just before brewing will do more for the cup than almost any other change. You can explore the full range in our [coffee beans](L2) collection.

## Cleaning and Care

A French press stays clean-tasting only if you clean it properly. Coffee oils cling to the mesh and plunger, and over time they turn rancid and give fresh brews a stale, bitter edge.

- **Discard the grounds** into a compost bin or rubbish bin, not down the sink, where they can build up and block drains.
- **Rinse right away** with warm water before the residue dries on.
- **Take it apart regularly.** All parts of our French Press come apart for cleaning, so you can unscrew the plunger and wash each mesh layer and plate separately [F8].
- **Wash with mild detergent** and a soft brush, then rinse thoroughly so no soapy taste remains.

Borosilicate glass handles heat well, but it can still break if dropped or knocked. The beaker on our French Press is replaceable, so a broken beaker does not mean replacing the whole brewer [F4, F9].

Once you are comfortable with the press, the same immersion principles carry over to other brewers in our [immersion brewers](L3) collection. Weigh your coffee, grind it coarse and even, steep with intent, press gently and pour straight away, and the French press will give you a cup that is both clean and full-bodied, every time.
